a: coat them with plaster
p: Ink on a fresh coat of lime plaster was a known way to put up a public text in the ancient Near East.
b: The Hebrew sid is lime plaster. Writing in ink or paint on plastered stone or walls was a common way to display a public text. The best-known example near Israel is the Balaam text from Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley (about 800 BC), painted in ink on a plastered wall. Egypt also painted texts on plastered surfaces. Such writing does not last long in rain, which may be why the stones are set up beside an altar and read aloud at a ceremony. The Mishnah says the words were written in seventy languages, so that every nation could read the law (Mishnah Sotah 7:5).

a: Write all the words of this law on them
t: What was written on the stones?
p: The whole book, the laws of chapters 12–26, or a short summary? The text does not say.
b: "This law" in Deuteronomy usually means Moses' teaching in this book (1:5; 4:44; 31:9). Even so, it is hard to picture all of Deuteronomy on a few stones. The rabbis held that the whole Torah was written, in seventy languages (Mishnah Sotah 7:5; Talmud Sotah 35b–36a). Many modern commentators think of the laws of chapters 12–26, or of the curses that follow in this chapter. Joshua 8:32 says Joshua wrote on the stones "a copy of the law of Moses." Ancient treaties also required that their text be written and displayed, so the stones work like a public copy of a covenant document.

a: Do not swing an iron tool over them
p: The same rule as the first altar law in Exodus 20:25. The rabbis said iron shortens life, and the altar lengthens it.
b: Exodus 20:25 forbids an altar of cut stone, because swinging a blade over it makes it unholy. Deuteronomy names the tool "iron." The stones must be "whole" (shelemot, verse 6), as God made them. The Mishnah explains that iron was made to shorten human life, while the altar was made to lengthen it, so it is not right to wave what shortens over what lengthens (Mishnah Middot 3:4). Joshua builds such an altar on Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:31), and 1 Kings 6:7 says no iron tool was heard at the temple site.

a: Build the altar of the LORD your God out of whole, uncut stones
t: An altar found on Mount Ebal?
p: In the 1980s Adam Zertal dug a stone structure on Ebal and called it Joshua's altar. Others disagree.
b: From 1982 Adam Zertal excavated a large rectangular stone structure on the northeast slope of Mount Ebal, dated to about 1200 BC, filled with ash and burned bones of young sheep, goats and cattle. He identified it as an Israelite altar, perhaps the one in Joshua 8:30–35. Aharon Kempinski answered that it was a watchtower or farmhouse, and the debate continues; Ralph Hawkins argues for a place of worship. In 2022 Scott Stripling's team announced a tiny folded lead tablet from Zertal's dump with a curse naming YHW. Many specialists say no letters can be read on it, so the claim remains disputed.

a: Be still and listen, Israel!
p: The verb for "be still" appears only here in the Bible. The rabbis read in it a call to form study groups.
b: Hasket means "be quiet, pay attention." It sits beside shema, "listen," as in the Shema (6:4). The words "today you have become the people" are surprising, since Israel became God's people at Sinai long before. The Talmud draws a lesson: the Torah should be as fresh to you every day as on the day it was given. It also plays on hasket as asu kitot, "make yourselves into groups," because Torah is learned best with others (Talmud Berakhot 63b).
orig: הַסְכֵּת (hasket), "be silent, attend"

a: these tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people
p: Gerizim and Ebal stand on either side of the pass at Shechem, a natural theater for a public ceremony.
b: Mount Gerizim (about 2,890 feet) rises south of the valley where Shechem lay, near modern Nablus, and Mount Ebal (about 3,080 feet) rises to the north. The slopes face each other across a narrow valley, and voices carry well between them. The six tribes on Gerizim are all sons of Jacob's wives Leah and Rachel. The six on Ebal are the four sons of the slave women Bilhah and Zilpah, plus Reuben, who lost his place as firstborn (Genesis 35:22; 49:4), and Zebulun, Leah's youngest. Joshua 8:33 carries out the ceremony, and Jotham shouts his fable from Gerizim (Judges 9:7).

a: Then the Levites will call out in a loud voice
p: Levi is listed on Gerizim (verse 12), yet here the Levites call out the curses. How do the two fit?
b: Verse 12 puts Levi among the tribes on Gerizim, but verse 14 has "the Levites" proclaiming the twelve curses to everyone. The Mishnah solves it this way: the priests and some Levites stood in the valley with the ark, turned toward one mountain for each blessing and toward the other for each curse, while all the people answered "Amen" (Mishnah Sotah 7:5). Critical scholars usually think two separate ceremonies have been joined: a blessing-and-curse rite on two mountains (27:11–13), and a liturgy of twelve curses led by Levites (27:14–26), which never says what the blessers said.

a: A curse on anyone who
p: The Hebrew arur declares a person cut off from blessing. Most of these sins are done where no court can see.
b: Arur is not a magic spell. It declares someone banned from the community's blessing and handed over to God's judgment. There are twelve curses, often taken as one for each tribe. They begin and end with acts "in secret" (verses 15 and 24) and close with the whole law (verse 26). Many interpreters notice that most are sins easily hidden: a private idol, a moved boundary marker, a misled blind man, incest at home, a bribe. Human judges may never learn of them, so the people put themselves under God's curse if they do them. Each curse matches a law elsewhere in the Torah.
orig: אָרוּר (arur), "cursed"

a: 'Amen!'
p: "Amen" means "firm, sure": by saying it, the people sign their names to each curse.
b: Amen comes from the root of words for firmness and trust (emunah, "faithfulness"). Said after a curse or an oath, it means "so be it, I accept it." A woman under suspicion says "Amen, amen" to the priest's curse (Numbers 5:22), and Nehemiah's people say it to an oath (Nehemiah 5:13). The word passed unchanged into Greek, Latin and English worship. Jesus begins his sayings with "Amen," and Revelation calls him "the Amen" (Revelation 3:14).
orig: אָמֵן (amen), "surely, so be it"
r: Numbers 5:22; Nehemiah 5:13; Nehemiah 8:6; 1 Chronicles 16:36; 2 Corinthians 1:20; Revelation 3:14

a: shifts his neighbor's boundary marker
p: In a farming world a field's edge was marked by stones. Babylonian boundary stones even carried curses.
b: A neighbor could gain land at night by moving a marker a few feet. The law is in 19:14, and Proverbs repeats it (Proverbs 22:28; Proverbs 23:10). The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope (about 1200 BC), which Proverbs 22–24 resembles, also warns against moving the markers on the edge of a field. In Babylon, land grants were recorded on carved boundary stones (kudurru) that called down the gods' curses on anyone who moved or erased them. Hosea compares Judah's leaders to those who move boundaries (Hosea 5:10).

a: sends a blind person the wrong way on the road
p: Leviticus 19:14 forbids setting something in a blind person's way. The rabbis applied it to bad advice.
b: This curse fits Leviticus 19:14, which forbids putting something to trip over in front of a blind person. The weak, who cannot see who harmed them, are under God's care. The rabbis widened both laws: to give someone advice you know is bad, or to tempt someone into a sin they are "blind" to, is to mislead the blind (Sifra on Leviticus 19:14). Jesus calls the religious leaders "blind guides" (Matthew 15:14; Matthew 23:16).

a: for he has lifted the wing of his father's cloak
p: Spreading a cloak's wing over a woman claimed her as a wife. To lift it back is to take what is the father's.
b: The kanaf is the corner or "wing" of a cloak. Ruth asks Boaz to spread his corner over her, a request for marriage (Ruth 3:9), and God spreads his over Jerusalem (Ezekiel 16:8). Here the son lifts the covering that belongs to his father, taking his father's wife. "Father's wife" usually means a stepmother, often a younger wife of a man with more than one. The same law and the same words appear in 22:30. Reuben did this with Bilhah (Genesis 35:22), and Paul condemns a case in Corinth (1 Corinthians 5:1).
orig: גִּלָּה כְּנַף אָבִיו (gillah kenaf aviv), "he uncovered his father's corner"
r: 22:30; Leviticus 18:8; Leviticus 20:11; Ruth 3:9; Ezekiel 16:8; Genesis 35:22; 1 Corinthians 5:1

a: whether she is his father's daughter or his mother's daughter
p: Abraham married his half-sister, and Tamar thought David might allow her marriage to Amnon. How old is this law?
b: This curse covers a half-sister as well as a full sister, as Leviticus 18:9 and 20:17 do. Yet Abraham says Sarah is "my father's daughter though not my mother's" (Genesis 20:12), and Tamar tells her half-brother Amnon that King David would let him marry her (2 Samuel 13:13). Traditional readers answer that Abraham lived before the law was given, and that Tamar was stalling for time. Many critical scholars take these stories as signs that such marriages were once allowed and that the laws in Leviticus and Deuteronomy are later.

a: attacks his neighbor where no one sees
p: The verb usually means to strike someone dead. Jewish tradition also read it as slander, a blow with the tongue.
b: Makkeh is "one who strikes," and in law it often means killing (Exodus 21:12). This curse covers the murder or assault that has no witnesses, which a court cannot punish (compare the unsolved killing in 21:1–9). Rashi, following earlier rabbis, reads it as slander: words that wound a neighbor behind his back. The Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan likewise speaks of striking "with the tongue." Both readings fit the theme of the curses, sins done "in secret."
orig: מַכֵּה רֵעֵהוּ בַּסָּתֶר (makkeh re'ehu basater), "one who strikes his neighbor in secret"

a: A curse on anyone who does not make the words of this law stand by doing them
t: Paul and the curse of the law
p: Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 3:10, then says Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).
b: Paul quotes it in a form close to the Greek: "Cursed is everyone who does not stay with all the things written in the book of the law, so as to do them" (Galatians 3:10). His point is that all who rely on "works of the law" stand under its curse, and then: "Christ bought us free from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us," citing 21:23. The traditional Protestant reading (Luther, Calvin, Moo) is that no one keeps the law perfectly. Others, such as N. T. Wright, read the curse as Israel's national exile, which Christ takes on himself. James Dunn reads "works of the law" as the marks that set Jews apart.

a: by doing them
p: A Talmud passage applies this verse to the one who lifts the Torah scroll before the congregation.
b: Ramban (Nachmanides) gives two Jewish readings of "make the words of this law stand." First, it curses anyone who denies that a single commandment is true, even if he slips in keeping it, since every person sometimes fails. Second, he cites the Jerusalem Talmud (Sotah 7:4): it refers to the synagogue official who does not lift the Torah scroll and show its writing to the congregation. That act, hagbahah, is still done after the Torah reading, so that everyone can see the words "standing."

a: If you truly listen to the LORD your God
p: Hebrew has no separate word for "obey." To listen truly is to do what you hear.
b: The Hebrew doubles the verb: shamoa tishma, "if listening you listen." Most English versions write "obey," which is the right sense, but the Hebrew keeps the picture of hearing a voice. The chapter turns on this word: the blessings come "if you listen" (28:1–2, 13), and the curses "if you will not listen" (28:15, 45, 62). It is the same verb as the Shema, "Listen, Israel" (6:4).
orig: שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמַע (shamoa tishma), "if you listen, listen"

a: the calves of your herds and the lambs of your flocks
p: The words for "calves" and "lambs" here are the names of the Canaanite gods Shegar and Astarte.
b: The Hebrew says shegar alafekha ve'ashterot tsonekha. Shegar was a god of animal offspring known from Ugarit and from the Deir Alla text, and Ashtarot is the plural of Astarte, the goddess of fertility. Here both have become ordinary farm words, "the young of the herd" and "the increase of the flock," in the way English "cereal" comes from the Roman goddess Ceres. Verdict: the link is real, but it is a matter of vocabulary. The point is that the LORD, not Shegar or Astarte, gives the newborn animals.
orig: שְׁגַר אֲלָפֶיךָ וְעַשְׁתְּרוֹת צֹאנֶךָ (shegar alafekha ve'ashterot tsonekha)

a: the LORD's name has been called over you
p: To call someone's name over a thing was to claim it as one's own property.
b: The idiom means ownership. Joab tells David to take a city himself, or it will be "called by my name" (2 Samuel 12:28). The temple is the house "called by my name" (Jeremiah 7:10), and Amos looks to the nations "over whom my name has been called" (Amos 9:12), a verse James quotes at the council in Jerusalem (Acts 15:17). So the nations will see that Israel belongs to the LORD, and they will fear to touch it.
orig: שֵׁם יְהוָה נִקְרָא עָלֶיךָ (shem YHWH niqra alekha), "the LORD's name is called over you"

a: But if you will not listen to the LORD your God
t: Reading the curses in the synagogue
p: Jews call this section the Tokhechah, "the rebuke," and read it quickly and quietly.
b: When the yearly cycle of Torah readings reaches 28:15–68, the reader lowers his voice and reads quickly. The Talmud forbids breaking up the curses of Leviticus 26 between two readers, but it allows a break here. Its reason: the Leviticus curses are in the plural and Moses spoke them from God's mouth, while these are in the singular and Moses said them on his own (Megillah 31b). Later custom treats both alike (Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 428:6), so one person takes them all, and often the reader himself is called up, since no one wants that portion. The curses run four times as long as the blessings (28:1–14), as in the treaties of the time (see 28:23).

a: when you abandoned me
p: In the middle of Moses' speech, the "me" is suddenly God. The speaker and the One he speaks for blur.
b: Moses has been speaking of "the LORD" in the third person, then the Hebrew says azavtani, "you abandoned me." The same happens in 29:5–6 ("I led you ... so you would learn that I am the LORD your God") and 11:14–15. Prophets often slip into God's first person as they speak his message. Several modern versions smooth it to "him." The Greek and Latin keep "me," and so does the Plain English Translation.
orig: עֲזַבְתָּנִי (azavtani), "you have forsaken me"

a: The sky above you will turn to bronze, and the ground below you to iron
p: An Assyrian treaty of 672 BC has almost the same curse. Leviticus 26:19 has it the other way around.
b: The loyalty oaths that King Esarhaddon of Assyria imposed on his vassals in 672 BC include a curse that the gods make the vassal's ground like iron, and that as rain does not fall from a sky of bronze, so rain and dew will not fall on his fields. Leviticus 26:19 has iron sky and bronze ground. Moshe Weinfeld and Hans Ulrich Steymans argue that Deuteronomy 28 borrows directly from such Assyrian oaths, which fits a date in the 7th century BC. Kenneth Kitchen answers that curse lists like this were used for centuries and appear in older Hittite and Aramean treaties. Verdict: a real connection to the treaty tradition, with the direction of borrowing debated.

a: with tumors
p: The written word here was read aloud as a politer word. The rabbis listed it among words "read more decently."
b: The consonants written in the text are ofalim, "swellings," a word thought crude, probably for hemorrhoids or sores in the private parts. The tradition reads it aloud as techorim, a more decent word for the same complaint (the KJV's "emerods"). Both likely mean the same ailment; only the tone differs. This is a ketiv (what is written) and qere (what is read). The Talmud says that every crude word written in the Torah is read in a cleaner way (Megillah 25b). The same pair appears in the Philistine plague of 1 Samuel 5–6. "Egypt's boils" recall the sixth plague (Exodus 9:9–11).
orig: ketiv עפלים (ofalim), qere טְּחֹרִים (techorim)

a: You will build a house and never live there
p: The war law excused a man who had a new house, vineyard or bride. Now enemies take all three.
b: In 20:5–7 the officers send home from battle any man who has built a house and not lived in it, planted a vineyard and not used it, or become engaged and not married. Here the same three blessings are taken by others. The prophets reuse these "futility curses": "you built houses of dressed stone, but you will not get to live in them" (Amos 5:11; Zephaniah 1:13). Isaiah reverses them in the new creation, where those who build will live in their houses (Isaiah 65:21–22).

a: with the king you put over yourselves
p: Israel has no king when Moses speaks. Readers have seen here Israel's kings led away by Assyria and Babylon.
b: The law of the king (17:14–20) imagines Israel choosing a king; now he goes into exile with his people. Hoshea of Israel was imprisoned by Assyria (2 Kings 17:4–6), King Manasseh was taken to Babylon in chains (2 Chronicles 33:11), and Jehoiachin and Zedekiah were deported by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 24:15; 2 Kings 25:7). Traditional readers see true prediction. Critical scholars usually date the passage after one of these events, or during the Assyrian threat of the late 8th or 7th century BC.

a: a sign and a wonder
p: "Signs and wonders" were what God did to Egypt. Now Israel itself becomes the sign.
b: Ot u-mofet, "a sign and a wonder," is Deuteronomy's phrase for the plagues of Egypt (4:34; 6:22; 7:19; 29:3; 34:11). Turned against Israel, it means that the people's suffering will be a lesson that everyone can read. The chapter is full of such reversals: the diseases of Egypt return (28:27, 60), and in the end the LORD sends Israel back to Egypt (28:68).
orig: לְאוֹת וּלְמוֹפֵת (le'ot ulemofet), "for a sign and a wonder"

a: It will dive on you the way an eagle swoops
p: Jeremiah uses these very words of Babylon. The Hebrew nesher may be an eagle or a griffon vulture.
b: A distant nation with a strange language, swooping like a bird of prey: the prophets apply this to Assyria and Babylon. Jeremiah warns, "I will bring a nation on you from far away... a nation from ancient times... a nation whose language you do not know" (Jeremiah 5:15), and Habakkuk says the Babylonians' horsemen fly "like an eagle hurrying to eat" (Habakkuk 1:8). Lamentations remembers pursuers "faster than eagles" (Lamentations 4:19). The nesher can be an eagle or the great griffon vulture, which fits a bird that comes to the dead. Paul's quotation about "strange tongues" (1 Corinthians 14:21) comes from Isaiah 28:11, which echoes this verse.
orig: נֶשֶׁר (nesher), "eagle, vulture"
r: Jeremiah 5:15; Jeremiah 48:40; Habakkuk 1:6–8; Lamentations 4:19; Isaiah 5:26–28; Isaiah 28:11; 1 Corinthians 14:21

a: you will eat your own children
p: The Bible and Josephus record that this horror really happened in the sieges of Samaria and Jerusalem.
b: Long sieges starved cities until people ate the unthinkable. In the Aramean siege of Samaria two mothers agree to eat their sons (2 Kings 6:24–29). Lamentations says that in Babylon's siege of Jerusalem tender-hearted women cooked their own children with their own hands (Lamentations 4:10; Lamentations 2:20). Josephus tells of a woman named Mary who did this during the Roman siege of AD 70 (Jewish War 6.201–213). Esarhaddon's treaty of 672 BC carries the same curse: that in their hunger the rebels will eat the flesh of their own sons. Leviticus 26:29 and Ezekiel 5:10 also threaten it.
r: Leviticus 26:29; 2 Kings 6:24–29; Lamentations 2:20; Lamentations 4:10; Ezekiel 5:10; Jeremiah 19:9

a: this scroll
t: A book that knows it is a book
p: From here on Deuteronomy speaks of itself as a written scroll, the first book of the Bible to do so.
b: The Hebrew sefer means any written document, and at this time it was a scroll of papyrus or leather. Deuteronomy refers to "this scroll" (28:58, 61; 29:20–21, 27; 30:10), tells how Moses wrote it and had it placed beside the ark (31:9, 24–26), and asks the king to copy it (17:18). Scholars of every school see this as the start of the idea of a written Scripture. Many critical scholars connect it with "the scroll of the law" found in the temple under King Josiah in 622 BC (2 Kings 22:8–13).
orig: הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה (hassefer hazzeh), "this book, this scroll"

a: this name full of glory and terror, the LORD your God
p: Deuteronomy speaks of God's name almost as a presence. Later Jews called God simply HaShem, "the Name."
b: The verse fears "this glorious and awesome name," and then spells it out: YHWH your God. Deuteronomy often says God will make "his name dwell" in the place he chooses (12:11). Out of reverence, Jews stopped saying the name YHWH aloud and replaced it with Adonai, "Lord," in prayer and HaShem, "the Name," in speech. That is why most English Bibles, including this one, print "the LORD" in small capitals. Leviticus 24:11–16 tells of a man who cursed "the Name."
orig: הַשֵּׁם הַנִּכְבָּד וְהַנּוֹרָא (hashem hannikhbad vehannora), "the glorious and fearful name"

a: so the LORD will rejoice over you as he ruins you and destroys you
t: Does God rejoice when people perish?
p: The rabbis said no: God does not rejoice, but he lets others rejoice. They read the verb as "he will cause to rejoice."
b: The Hebrew verb is yasis, which the Talmud reads as causative: "he will make others rejoice," not "he will rejoice" (Megillah 10b; Sanhedrin 39b). There the rabbis tell how, when the Egyptians drowned in the sea, the angels wanted to sing, and God said: "My handiwork is drowning in the sea, and you want to sing?" They also cite Proverbs 24:17 and Ezekiel 18:23, "Is it the death of the wicked that I really take pleasure in?" Most modern scholars take the verb simply as "he will rejoice," a bold statement that God's justice is as willing as his goodness.

a: The LORD will scatter you among all the peoples
p: Ramban read Leviticus 26 as the Babylonian exile and Deuteronomy 28 as the long exile after Rome.
b: Many Jewish readers have seen their whole history in this chapter: scattering "from one end of the earth to the other," no rest, life in constant fear. Ramban (Nachmanides, 13th century) argued that the curses of Leviticus 26 describe the first exile, which ended after seventy years, while Deuteronomy 28 describes the second exile, after the Romans destroyed the temple, which has no stated end. Christian writers too have often pointed to the Jewish dispersion, at times cruelly, as fulfillment. Critical scholars read the verse against the Assyrian and Babylonian deportations.

a: there will be no place for the sole of your foot to stop
p: The same words describe Noah's dove, which found nowhere to land.
b: "No place to rest the sole of its foot" is said of the dove sent out from the ark (Genesis 8:9). The exiled people will be like the dove over the flood waters, with nowhere to settle. Lamentations says Judah "She lives among the nations and has found no place to rest" (Lamentations 1:3). The promise of the land had been a promise of "rest" (12:9–10); exile undoes it.

a: Your life will hang in front of you by a thread
p: Early Christians read the Greek of this verse as a picture of Christ hanging on the cross.
b: The Hebrew means life in suspense, never sure of the next day. The Talmud gives homely examples. Life hanging in doubt is the person who has no field and must buy a year's grain; fear by night and day is the one who buys from week to week; and no confidence in life is the one who depends on the baker (Menachot 103b). The Greek says "your life will be hanging before your eyes." Melito of Sardis (Peri Pascha 61), Tertullian (Against the Jews 11) and others read this as a prophecy of Christ, "our life," hung on the cross before Israel's eyes. Modern Christian scholars generally treat that as a later use of the words, not their first meaning.

a: The LORD will ship you back to Egypt
p: The last curse undoes the exodus. Josephus says Titus sent Jewish captives to Egypt after AD 70.
b: God had said Israel would never return to Egypt (17:16; Exodus 14:13). The final curse reverses the whole story: back to Egypt, in ships, as slaves, and so worthless that no one will buy them. After Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, many Judeans fled to Egypt (Jeremiah 43–44). Josephus reports that after the war of AD 70 Titus sent captives over seventeen to forced labor in Egypt, and that the slave markets were so full that buyers were few (Jewish War 6.384, 418). Hosea had warned, "They will return to Egypt" (Hosea 8:13; Hosea 9:3).

a: besides the covenant he had made with them at Horeb
p: In Hebrew this verse is 28:69, the end of chapter 28. Is the covenant in Moab new, or Horeb renewed?
b: Hebrew Bibles number this verse 28:69, so it closes the speech of chapters 5–28 ("these are the words of the covenant"). English Bibles, following the Greek and Latin, make it the heading of chapters 29–30. Either way it names a covenant "in the land of Moab" besides the one at Horeb (Sinai). The rabbis counted covenants at Horeb, in Moab and at Mount Ebal (Talmud Sotah 37b). Most interpreters see a renewal of the Sinai covenant with the new generation, as ancient kings renewed treaties with a vassal's heir. Some critical scholars see a distinct "Moab covenant" theology written for exiles.

a: Yet to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to know with, eyes to see with or ears to hear with
p: Paul joins this verse to Isaiah 29:10 to explain why most of Israel did not believe in Jesus (Romans 11:8).
b: Moses says the people saw the wonders but did not understand them, because understanding is God's gift. Isaiah's call uses the same pair of eyes and ears (Isaiah 6:9–10), and Jesus quotes it of those who hear his parables (Matthew 13:13–15). Paul combines this verse and Isaiah 29:10: "God gave them a spirit of numbness: eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, down to this very day" (Romans 11:8). Rashi notes "until today": only after forty years does a student fully grasp his teacher's mind (Talmud Avodah Zarah 5b).

a: All of you stand here today before the LORD your God
p: The Torah portion Nitzavim, "standing," begins here. It is read on the Sabbath before the Jewish New Year.
b: Atem nitzavim hayyom, "you are standing today," names the weekly portion 29:10–30:20, read just before Rosh Hashanah, when Jews prepare to stand before God in judgment. The list runs from chiefs to water carriers, with women, children and foreigners included: the covenant binds the whole community, not only its men. Rashi identifies the woodcutters and water carriers as Canaanites who came to join Israel in Moses' time, as the Gibeonites later did by a trick (Joshua 9:21–27).

a: and his curse-oath
p: The Hebrew alah is an oath that calls down a curse on the one who breaks it.
b: Hebrew joins berit, "covenant," with alah, "oath with a curse" (also 29:14, 19, 21). A covenant was sworn under curse: "may this happen to me if I break it." The people are told to "cross over" into it, which may recall ceremonies where those making the covenant walked between cut animals (Genesis 15:17; Jeremiah 34:18–20). The same pair appears in Isaac's treaty with Abimelech (Genesis 26:28) and in Ezekiel 17:13–19.
orig: בִּבְרִית ... וּבְאָלָתוֹ (bivrit ... uve'alato), "into the covenant ... and into its curse-oath"

a: and for the one who is not here with us today
p: The rabbis taught that the souls of all future Jews, and of all future converts, stood at this covenant.
b: The covenant reaches people not yet born. The Talmud says that when Moses made Israel swear, he swore them "not on your own minds but on the mind of God," and the oath bound "those who stood at Mount Sinai and the generations to come, and the converts who would later convert" (Shevuot 39a). The midrash adds that all the souls of later generations were present (Tanhuma Nitzavim). Christians in the Reformed tradition have used the verse to argue that covenant promises include the children of believers.

a: their loathsome things and their idols
p: Gillulim, a common word for idols, probably meant "dung-things." Shiqqutsim means "disgusting things."
b: Hebrew had insulting names for other peoples' gods. Shiqqutsim means "detestable things," the word for unclean food (Leviticus 11:10–11). Gillulim sounds like gel, "dung," and like "round lumps," so it may have meant "dung pellets." Ezekiel uses it nearly forty times. The list "wood and stone, silver and gold" mocks gods that are only material, as in 4:28 and Psalm 115:4–8.
orig: שִׁקּוּצֵיהֶם ... גִּלֻּלֵיהֶם (shiqqutsehem ... gillulehem)

a: no root is here among you that bears poison and wormwood
p: Hebrews 12:15 warns against a "root of bitterness" springing up, from the Greek of this verse.
b: Wormwood (la'anah) is a bitter plant, a picture for something that ruins from within. The Greek reads "a root growing up in gall and bitterness," and Hebrews 12:15 warns that no "root of bitterness" spring up and cause trouble. The Hebrews wording matches Codex Alexandrinus, which reads "cause trouble" (enochlē) where Vaticanus has "in gall" (en cholē). The two differ by one transposed letter, and many think Alexandrinus was conformed to Hebrews. Revelation's star "Wormwood" turns waters bitter (Revelation 8:11), and Amos says Israel has turned justice to wormwood (Amos 5:7).
r: Hebrews 12:15; Amos 5:7; Amos 6:12; Jeremiah 9:15; Lamentations 3:19; Revelation 8:11

a: That would sweep away the watered ground along with the dry
p: A famous puzzle. It may be a saying for "everything," or the sinner may drag the whole community down.
b: The Hebrew sefot ha-ravah et ha-tseme'ah is literally "to sweep away the watered with the thirsty." Three main readings: (1) a proverb for total destruction, "wet and dry alike," so one secret idolater brings ruin on all; (2) the man's own words, "I will add drunkenness to thirst" (KJV), meaning he will indulge himself freely; (3) the Targum's "to add sins done by mistake to sins done on purpose." Rashi takes it as God adding punishment for the man's earlier sins. The Plain English Translation gives the literal picture.
orig: סְפוֹת הָרָוָה אֶת־הַצְּמֵאָה (sefot ha-ravah et ha-tseme'ah)

a: Every curse written in this scroll will crouch on him
p: The verb is used of an animal lying down on its prey, the same picture as sin crouching in Genesis 4:7.
b: Ravtsah is what an animal does when it lies down, and Genesis 4:7 uses it for sin "crouching at the door." The curse is pictured as a beast settling on the one man who thought he could hide. The "smoke" of God's anger in the same verse is another vivid picture (Psalm 74:1). "Wipe out his name" means he will have no descendants to carry his memory (25:6; Psalm 109:13).
orig: וְרָבְצָה בּוֹ (veravtsah bo), "and it will crouch on him"

a: Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim
p: Admah and Zeboiim were Sodom's neighbors (Genesis 14:2). Their landscape of salt and sulfur was proverbial.
b: Genesis names four cities by the Dead Sea: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim (Genesis 10:19; Genesis 14:2, 8), and Genesis 19 tells of sulfur and fire raining on them. The salt flats and sulfur deposits around the Dead Sea made the region a picture of ruin that never recovers. Hosea uses Admah and Zeboiim when God says he cannot destroy Ephraim like them (Hosea 11:8). Jeremiah and Zephaniah use Sodom for Edom, Moab and Babylon.
r: Genesis 10:19; Genesis 14:2; Genesis 19:24–28; Hosea 11:8; Jeremiah 49:18; Zephaniah 2:9; Amos 4:11

a: Every nation will ask, 'Why did the LORD treat this land this way?
p: An Assyrian royal text has defeated Arabs ask the same question, and give the same answer: they broke their oath.
b: In the annals of Ashurbanipal of Assyria (7th century BC), Arabs who rebelled ask one another why such evil has come on Arabia, and answer that they did not keep the great oaths sworn by Ashur. Moshe Weinfeld pointed out how close this is to 29:24–28 and to 1 Kings 9:8–9 and Jeremiah 22:8–9. Verdict: a shared Near Eastern way of explaining disaster as punishment for breaking a sworn treaty. In Israel's version the broken oath is with the LORD, and the wrong is serving other gods.

a: gods he had not assigned to them
p: The verb means "allot, give as a share." It assumes the picture of 4:19 and 32:8–9.
b: Chalaq is to divide a share or inheritance. In 4:19 Moses says the LORD has given the sun, moon and stars "as a share to all the peoples under the whole sky", while he took Israel for himself. Here the gods Israel turned to were not Israel's share. The Song makes it a scene: the Most High divides the nations by the number of the "sons of God," but keeps Jacob as his own portion (32:8–9). Jewish and Christian readers have long debated whether these "gods" are angels set over the nations, demons, or simply idols (see 32:8).
orig: וְלֹא חָלַק לָהֶם (velo chalaq lahem), "and he did not allot to them"

a: flung them into another land, where they are today
t: The large letter and the lost tribes
p: Torah scrolls write the first letter of "flung them" extra large. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer read "today" differently.
b: In Hebrew this is 29:27, and scribes write the lamed of vayyashlikhem, "he flung them," oversized. The Mishnah records a debate over the ten northern tribes taken by Assyria. Rabbi Akiva said, "As this day goes and does not return, so they went and will not return." Rabbi Eliezer answered, "As the day grows dark and then becomes light, so for the ten tribes: darkness now, light later" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:3). "Where they are today" also sounds like someone writing after the exile had happened, a point critical scholars make.

a: What has been made known is for us and our children for all time
p: The Masoretes put dots over eleven letters in this verse, an old scribal sign whose meaning was debated.
b: Over "for us and for our children" and the first letter of "forever," Hebrew manuscripts have puncta extraordinaria, special dots, one of ten such places in the Torah. Such dots often marked letters a scribe doubted. The Talmud reads a lesson: Israel was not punished as a community for hidden sins until it crossed the Jordan and took the oath at Ebal and Gerizim, but for open sins it was responsible from the start (Sanhedrin 43b). Modern scholars think the dots began as a scribal note on the text, its meaning since lost.
orig: לָנוּ וּלְבָנֵינוּ עַד (lanu ulevanenu ad), with dots over each letter

a: What is hidden is for the LORD our God
p: The verse marks the limit of what humans can know, and points them back to what God has made plain.
b: Read with 29:19–28, "what is hidden" may be the secret sin of one person, which God alone sees and judges, while the community must act on what is known. Read on its own, it became a principle about knowledge of God: what God has not revealed is his business, and what he has revealed is ours to do. Calvin used it to warn against prying into God's hidden decree of predestination (Institutes 3.21.3). Jewish readers have cited it against speculation about the end and about God's reasons for the commandments.

a: you will take them to heart
t: A promise that Israel will return
p: Maimonides read chapter 30 as a promise: Israel will repent at the end of its exile and be redeemed at once.
b: Literally "you will bring them back to your heart." Is this a condition ("if you return") or a prediction ("you will return")? The Hebrew allows both, and readers divide. Maimonides wrote that "the Torah has already promised that Israel will repent at the end of its exile and will be redeemed immediately," citing 30:1–3 (Laws of Repentance 7:5). Many Christian readers see the restoration of Israel here too (Romans 11:25–27), while others apply it to every sinner who turns back. Critical scholars read 30:1–10 as written for exiles in Babylon.

a: the LORD your God will turn back your captivity
p: The verb shuv, "turn, return," appears seven times in 30:1–10. The rabbis read here that God goes into exile too.
b: Shav et shevutekha plays on one root: God will "turn the turning" of Israel. It can mean "bring back your captives" (KJV) or "restore your fortunes" (as in Job 42:10). The verb shuv runs through the passage: Israel turns back (30:2, 8, 10), and God turns back to them (30:3, 9). The Talmud notes that the verb is not "he will bring back" but "he will return," and concludes that God's presence went into exile with Israel and will come back with them (Megillah 29a).
orig: וְשָׁב ... אֶת־שְׁבוּתְךָ (veshav ... et shevutekha)

a: Even if you have been driven to the farthest edge of the sky
t: Gathered from the ends of heaven
p: Jesus uses the same picture: the angels will gather the chosen from one end of heaven to the other.
b: "The edge of the sky" is the horizon, the farthest place on earth. Nehemiah prays this promise back to God (Nehemiah 1:9). Jesus says the Son of Man will send his angels to gather his chosen "from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other" (Matthew 24:31; Mark 13:27). The daily Jewish prayer, the Amidah, asks God to "gather us together from the four corners of the earth."

a: The LORD your God will circumcise your heart
p: In 10:16 Israel is told to circumcise its own heart. Here God promises to do it.
b: A "circumcised heart" is one that is open and responsive to God; an "uncircumcised" heart is closed (Leviticus 26:41). The command in 10:16 becomes a promise here, the seed of the new covenant: Jeremiah 31:33 (the law written on the heart) and Ezekiel 36:26 (a new heart). Paul says true circumcision is "of the heart, in spirit and not in letter" (Romans 2:29; Colossians 2:11). Ramban wrote that this verse describes the days of the Messiah, when people will do good by nature and the evil inclination will lose its power.
r: 10:16; Leviticus 26:41; Jeremiah 4:4; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26; Romans 2:29; Colossians 2:11

a: It is not in the sky
p: In a famous Talmud story, rabbis outvote a voice from heaven by quoting this verse.
b: In the "oven of Akhnai" story (Bava Metzia 59b), Rabbi Eliezer proves his ruling with miracles and finally a voice from heaven. Rabbi Joshua stands up and says, "It is not in heaven!" The Torah has been given to humans, and its meaning is decided by the sages' majority (Exodus 23:2), not by heavenly voices. Elijah later reports that God laughed and said, "My children have defeated me." The story shows how Jews read this verse: God's word was handed over to be studied and applied on earth.

a: The word is close by you, very close: in your mouth and in your heart, for you to do
p: Paul reads verses 12–14 as about Christ and "the word of faith" (Romans 10:6–8).
b: Moses says God's command needs no hero to fetch it from heaven or across the sea. Baruch 3:29–30 applies the words to Wisdom, and Targum Neofiti mentions Moses going up to heaven and Jonah going down into the sea. Paul reworks them: no one needs to go up to bring Christ down or go down into the abyss to bring him up from the dead, for "Near you is the word, in your mouth and in your heart" (Romans 10:8), the message that Jesus is Lord, confessed and believed. Scholars debate how freely Paul is using the passage; Richard Hays argues that he hears in it the gospel of a word God has brought near.

a: Today I call the heavens and the earth to testify against you
p: Treaties called the gods, and also heaven and earth, as witnesses. Israel's covenant can call only creation.
b: Hittite treaties close with long lists of gods who witness the oath, ending with the mountains, the rivers, the springs, the great sea, heaven and earth, the winds and the clouds. Esarhaddon's oaths also invoke the gods of heaven and earth. Israel cannot call other gods to witness, so Moses calls heaven and earth themselves (4:26; 31:28; 32:1). The prophets later open their "lawsuits" against Israel in the same way (Isaiah 1:2; Micah 6:1–2). Verdict: a clear borrowing of treaty form, with the gods removed.

a: Choose life
p: The verse became a key text in debates over free will, from Sirach to Erasmus and Luther.
b: Sirach 15:15–17 echoes it: "If you choose, you can keep the commandments ... he has set before you fire and water." The Didache opens, "There are two ways, one of life and one of death." In 1524 Erasmus cited this verse to show that people can choose to turn to God. Luther replied in The Bondage of the Will (1525) that a command shows what we ought to do, not what we can do without grace. Jewish thought has generally read it as Maimonides did: every person has freedom to choose good or evil. Moses' "then" connects choice to love and to holding on to God (30:20).

a: He is your life
p: Rabbi Akiva used this verse to explain why Jews kept studying Torah under Roman persecution.
b: The Hebrew can mean "he is your life" (God) or "it is your life" (loving and holding on to him). Rabbi Akiva, when Rome forbade Torah study, told a parable. A fox invites the fish to escape the nets by coming up on dry land. The fish answer: if we are afraid in the water where we live, how much more on land, where we die? So too Israel: if we are in danger while studying Torah, of which it is written "it is your life and the length of your days," how much worse if we stop (Berakhot 61b).

a: Today I am a hundred and twenty years old
p: Jews still wish one another long life "until 120," the age of Moses.
b: Genesis 6:3 sets human days at 120 years, and Moses reaches that limit exactly. Acts 7:23 and 7:30 divide his life into three forties: forty in Egypt, forty in Midian, forty in the wilderness. The Sifre adds that Hillel, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and Rabbi Akiva each lived 120 years in three stages, like Moses (Sifre Deuteronomy 357). Hence the Jewish birthday wish, "May you live to 120."

a: I am no longer able to go out and come in
p: The phrase means leading the people, especially in war. It sits oddly beside 34:7, which says his vigor never failed.
b: To "go out and come in" before the people means to lead them on campaign (Numbers 27:17; 1 Samuel 18:16). But 34:7 says Moses' strength never failed. Rashi resolves it: Moses was able, but no longer permitted, because the leadership was passing to Joshua. Others say verse 2 is Moses' modest self-description, or that he means the closing of his own life. Critical scholars think different writers are at work.
orig: לָצֵאת וְלָבוֹא (latset velavo), "to go out and to come in"

a: He will not let you down, and he will not abandon you
p: Hebrews 13:5 quotes this promise. It is repeated to Joshua and by David to Solomon.
b: The promise is said twice in this chapter (31:6, 8), God adds his own pledge to be with Joshua (31:23), and it is said again to Joshua in Joshua 1:5. David passes it to Solomon as he builds the temple (1 Chronicles 28:20). Hebrews turns it into God's own word to every believer, in an emphatic Greek form: "I will never let you down, and I will never abandon you" (Hebrews 13:5), as a reason to be content and free from the love of money.

a: Be strong and bold
p: The words to Joshua became the cry of a synagogue at the end of each book of the Torah.
b: Chazaq ve'emats, "be strong and bold," is said to Joshua here and four times in Joshua 1. When a congregation finishes reading one of the five books of Moses, everyone stands and calls out Chazak, chazak, venitchazek, "Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another," before beginning the next book. Hezekiah uses the same words to his officers (2 Chronicles 32:7).

a: Moses put this law in writing
p: The book says Moses wrote "this law." Traditions differ on what that covers.
b: "This law" here means at least the speeches of Deuteronomy. Jewish and Christian tradition took it, with Exodus 24:4, as proof that Moses wrote the Torah. The Talmud says Moses wrote his book and the Balaam story, apart from the last eight verses, which Joshua wrote (Bava Batra 14b–15a). Most critical scholars see "Moses wrote" as the book's way of claiming Moses' authority for teaching written down much later, perhaps in the 7th century BC (see 28:58). Many evangelical scholars hold that the core is Mosaic, with later editing such as the account of his death.

a: in the Year of Release, when the Feast of Booths comes round
p: The Mishnah tells how King Agrippa read Deuteronomy to the people and wept at one verse.
b: Every seventh year, the year when debts were released (15:1–11), the whole people gathered at the Feast of Booths to hear the law. The Mishnah calls this Hakhel, "Gather!" (Mishnah Sotah 7:8). The king read from Deuteronomy on a wooden platform in the temple court. When King Agrippa (probably Agrippa I, AD 41–44) reached "You may not put over you a foreigner" (17:15), he wept, since his family was from Edom. The people called out, "Do not fear, you are our brother!" Nehemiah 8 shows a reading of this kind at Booths. Modern Israel has revived a Hakhel ceremony in Jerusalem.

a: the men, the women and the children
p: The Talmud asks why infants come to hear the law, and answers: to reward those who bring them.
b: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah taught: "The men come to learn, the women come to hear, but why do the little ones come? To give a reward to those who bring them" (Talmud Chagigah 3a). Modern readers note that the verse expects the youngest to be present and to grow up hearing (31:13). Women and foreigners are included, as in 29:11.

a: the tent of meeting
t: The tent of meeting in Deuteronomy
p: This is the only mention in Deuteronomy of the tent of meeting, and of the pillar of cloud there.
b: Elsewhere Deuteronomy speaks of the ark and "the place the LORD will choose," never of the tabernacle. Here, suddenly, the LORD appears in the pillar of cloud at the tent's entrance, as in Exodus 33:7–11 and Numbers 11:16–17 and 12:5, where the tent stands outside the camp and Joshua guards it. Critical scholars assign 31:14–15 and 31:23 to an older source (often called E) placed into Deuteronomy. Traditional readers see Moses and Joshua simply going to the tent, as they had done before.

a: You are about to lie down with your ancestors, and this people will rise up
p: The rabbis noticed that "rise up" could go with Moses: "you will lie down with your fathers and rise."
b: The Hebrew word veqam, "and will rise," stands between "you will lie down with your ancestors" and "this people." The Talmud lists it among five verses whose word order is undecided (Yoma 52a–b). When Romans challenged Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah to prove from the Torah that God raises the dead, he quoted, "You will lie down with your fathers and rise" (Sanhedrin 90b). He admitted the second half of the verse makes another reading possible. Most read the plain sense as "this people will rise up."

a: hide my face from them
p: Hester panim, "the hiding of the face," became a Jewish way of speaking about God's silence, even after the Holocaust.
b: For God to hide his face is to withdraw his care and protection, leaving people to the disasters that come (31:17–18; 32:20; Isaiah 54:8; Psalm 30:7). The Talmud finds a hint of Esther, a book where God is never named, in the Hebrew astir, "I will hide" (Chullin 139b). After the Holocaust, Jewish thinkers took up the phrase. Martin Buber wrote of an "eclipse of God," and Eliezer Berkovits argued that God hides his face so that human freedom can exist, even when humans abuse it.
orig: הִסְתַּרְתִּי פָנַי (histarti fanai), "I will hide my face"
r: 32:20; Isaiah 8:17; Isaiah 54:8; Psalm 13:1; Psalm 30:7; Ezekiel 39:23–24; Esther 4:14

a: So now write down this song for yourselves
p: The rabbis read "write for yourselves" as a command to every Jew: write your own Torah scroll.
b: The verb is plural, so the command is to Moses and Joshua. But the Talmud reads it as addressed to all Israel and to "this song" as the whole Torah, since the Torah may not be written in pieces. So every Jew must write, or have written, a Torah scroll (Sanhedrin 21b). It is the last commandment in the Torah's order (Sefer HaChinukh 613); Maimonides lists it as positive commandment 18 (Sefer HaMitzvot). Today a community often commissions a scroll together, and members each fill in a letter.

a: I know the plans they are shaping even today
p: Yetser, "what is formed, inclination," is the word behind the rabbis' "evil inclination."
b: Yitsro, literally "his forming," comes from the verb for a potter shaping clay. Genesis says the "inclination" of the human heart is only evil (Genesis 6:5; Genesis 8:21). The rabbis built on this word their teaching of two inclinations in every person, the yetzer hara (evil inclination) and yetzer hatov (good inclination). Here it means what Israel is already planning in its heart, before it even enters the land.
orig: יִצְרוֹ (yitsro), "its inclination, its forming"

a: Then he put Joshua son of Nun in charge
p: The Hebrew says only "he." The words "the land I swore" show that the speaker is the LORD.
b: The subject of "he put in charge" is not named, and the last person named is Moses (31:22). But the charge says "the land I swore to them, and I myself will be with you," which only God can say. So the verse goes back to 31:14–15, where God told Moses to bring Joshua to the tent "so that I can put him in charge." The Greek smooths this by naming Moses as the speaker and turning God's words into "the land the Lord swore" and "he will be with you." Many critical scholars think 31:14–15 and 31:23 were once one passage, with the song's introduction placed between them.
orig: וַיְצַו (vaytsav), "and he commanded, commissioned"

a: put it beside the ark
p: The rabbis debated whether the Torah scroll lay inside the ark with the tablets or on a ledge beside it.
b: The ark held the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments (10:1–5). Where did the scroll go? The Talmud reports a debate: Rabbi Meir said it lay inside the ark next to the tablets; Rabbi Judah said a board stuck out from the side of the ark and the scroll lay on it (Bava Batra 14a–b). 1 Kings 8:9 says nothing was in the ark but the two tablets. Many scholars connect the scroll "found" in the temple under Josiah with a copy kept in this way (2 Kings 22:8).

a: In the last days
p: Acharit hayyamim can mean "later on" or "the end of time." Context decides.
b: The phrase means literally "the end of the days." In the Torah it usually means "in time to come" (Genesis 49:1; Numbers 24:14; 4:30), and here it is the time after Moses' death when Israel will fall away. In the prophets it comes to mean the final age (Isaiah 2:2; Daniel 10:14), and the New Testament says the "last days" have begun with Jesus (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). The Plain English Translation keeps "last days" so the link can be seen; the sense here is "the days to come."
orig: בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים (be'acharit hayyamim), "at the end of the days"
r: 4:30; Genesis 49:1; Numbers 24:14; Isaiah 2:2; Daniel 10:14; Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2

a: the whole assembly of Israel
p: Qahal, "assembly," was translated ekklesia in Greek, the word the New Testament uses for "church."
b: Deuteronomy calls Israel gathered before God the qahal (5:22; 9:10; 23:1–8). The Septuagint often translated it ekklesia, "assembly," and Stephen speaks of "the assembly in the wilderness" (Acts 7:38). The early Christians called their own gatherings by the same word, which English renders "church." Israel had to be gathered as a whole to hear the song, as it was at Sinai.
orig: קְהַל יִשְׂרָאֵל (qehal yisra'el), "the assembly of Israel"

a: Listen closely, you heavens, and let me speak
p: The Song opens like a court case, calling heaven and earth as witnesses. Jews name it from its first word, Ha'azinu.
b: Ha'azinu, "listen," gives the Song (32:1–43) its Jewish name, and it is the weekly reading just after Nitzavim. Torah scrolls set it out in two columns. G. Ernest Wright (1962) called it a covenant "lawsuit" (Hebrew riv): witnesses are summoned (verse 1), God's past goodness is recalled (verses 7–14), Israel is accused (15–18) and sentenced (19–25), and then comes a surprise, God's mercy and vengeance on the enemy (26–43). Isaiah 1:2 opens with the same summons to heaven and earth. Dates proposed for the Song run from the 11th century BC (Otto Eissfeldt, W. F. Albright) to the exile; Paul Sanders' detailed study (1996) argues that it is older than the exile.

a: Let my teaching come down like rain
p: Words that soak in slowly and make things grow. The word for "teaching" is a word of the wisdom books.
b: Leqach, "teaching, what is received," belongs to the vocabulary of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:5; Proverbs 4:2), and some scholars see wisdom influence in the Song. Rain and dew bring life to the dry land of Israel, where everything depends on them (11:14). Isaiah says God's word comes down like rain and does not return empty (Isaiah 55:10–11). The Sifre compares the Torah to rain and dew, which all creatures need.

a: For I will call out the name of the LORD
p: The rabbis learned from this verse to say a blessing before reading the Torah, and to answer when God's name is spoken.
b: The Talmud derives the blessing said before reading Torah from this verse: when Moses proclaims the Name, the people answer, "Tell how great our God is" (Berakhot 21a). In the temple, when the high priest spoke the divine name on the Day of Atonement, the people responded, "Blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever and ever" (Yoma 37a, which also cites this verse). In the synagogue, the reader's "Bless the LORD" is still answered by the congregation.

a: He is the Rock
p: "Rock" is the Song's main name for God, used of the LORD and of other gods. The Greek replaced it with "God."
b: Tsur means a rock face or cliff, a place of safety in a land of ravines. The Song uses it for God again and again (32:4, 15, 18, 30, 31, 37), and once for real rock (32:13). Names like Elizur (Numbers 1:5), meaning "my God is a rock," show it was an old title. The Septuagint usually translates it "God," probably to avoid calling God a stone. Paul says of the rock that followed Israel, "the rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). Tamim, "flawless," is the word for an offering without defect.
orig: הַצּוּר תָּמִים פָּעֳלוֹ (hatsur tamim po'olo), "the Rock, flawless is his work"

a: he is fair and he is straight
p: Jewish burial prayers begin with this verse: God's justice is accepted even in grief.
b: The prayer Tziduk ha-Din, "declaring the judgment just," said at a Jewish burial, opens with "The Rock, flawless is his work, for all his ways are justice." The Talmud tells that when Rabbi Hanina ben Teradion and his family were condemned by Rome, he, his wife and his daughter each quoted a verse accepting God's justice, and he quoted this one (Avodah Zarah 18a). The verse answers the Song's later charge: the fault is Israel's, not God's (32:5).

a: they are not his children, they are a blot
p: The Hebrew here is very hard. Philippians 2:15 picks up its last line, "a crooked and twisted generation."
b: Word for word: "he/it ruined to him, not his sons, their blemish, a generation twisted and crooked." The grammar does not run smoothly, and translations guess: "they are no longer his children" (the blemish is why), "the blemish is theirs, not his children's" (KJV), or, with a small change, "his non-children have acted corruptly." The Greek has "they sinned, not his children, a blameworthy generation." The sense is clear: Israel spoiled its bond with God. Philippians 2:15 calls believers to shine "in a crooked and twisted generation," and Peter's sermon echoes the phrase (Acts 2:40).
orig: שִׁחֵת לוֹ לֹא בָּנָיו מוּמָם (shichet lo lo banav mumam)

a: Isn't he your father, who brought you into being
p: God as Israel's father. The verb qanah can mean "create" or "acquire," as with a purchase.
b: God is called Israel's father in Exodus 4:22 ("Israel is my son, my firstborn"), Isaiah 63:16 and Malachi 2:10. Qanah usually means "buy, acquire," but in Genesis 14:19, 22 God is qoneh of heaven and earth, and Wisdom says the LORD "brought me forth" (Proverbs 8:22), so many take it here as "create." Either way, Israel owes its existence to God, which makes its ingratitude foolish. Jesus' "Our Father" draws on this way of speaking.
orig: הֲלוֹא־הוּא אָבִיךָ קָּנֶךָ (halo hu avikha qanekha)
r: Exodus 4:22; Exodus 15:16; Isaiah 63:16; Isaiah 64:8; Malachi 2:10; Genesis 14:19; Proverbs 8:22

a: When the Most High handed out the nations' inheritance
t: The Most High divides the nations
p: The Most High (Elyon) gives each nation its land and its divine ruler, and keeps Israel for himself. Who is Elyon?
b: Elyon, "Most High," is an old divine title, known outside the Bible from the Aramaic Sefire treaty (8th century BC), which pairs "El and Elyon," and from Philo of Byblos. In the texts from Ugarit (about 1300 BC) the high god El has seventy sons. Genesis 10 lists seventy nations. Jewish tradition says God set an angel over each nation but ruled Israel himself (Sirach 17:17; Jubilees 15:31–32; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan here; compare Daniel 10:13, 20). Most interpreters, Jewish, Christian and critical, take Elyon as the LORD himself (verse 9 says "the LORD's own share"). Some critical scholars, such as Mark Smith, think the poem once pictured El dividing the nations among his sons, with YHWH receiving Israel. See the variant on "sons of God."
r: Genesis 10:1–32; Genesis 14:18–22; Psalm 82:1–8; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20; Acts 17:26; 4:19; 29:26

a: in a waste where the wild winds howl
p: The Song never mentions Egypt or the exodus. God "finds" Israel in the desert.
b: The Song tells Israel's story from God's finding it in the wilderness, with no slavery in Egypt, no plagues and no Sinai. Hosea 9:10 also says God "found Israel like grapes in the wilderness," and Jeremiah 2:2 remembers the desert as a honeymoon. Some critical scholars think this reflects an old tradition in which Israel's story began in the wilderness. Most traditional readers see poetic selection: the Song begins with God's care after the exodus. Ezekiel 16 tells a similar story of a foundling God picks up and raises.

a: he guarded him like the pupil of his eye
p: The Hebrew says "the little man of his eye," the tiny image of yourself you see in another's pupil.
b: Ishon is "little man," the pupil, where a person looking close sees his own reflection. The pupil is the most guarded part of the body: the eyelid closes at once to protect it. Old English called the pupil "the apple" of the eye, hence the King James "apple of his eye." The same picture appears in Psalm 17:8, Proverbs 7:2 and Zechariah 2:8, where "whoever touches you touches the pupil of his eye."
orig: כְּאִישׁוֹן עֵינוֹ (ke'ishon eino), "like the little man of his eye"

a: and hovers over its young
p: The verb is the one used for the Spirit "hovering" over the waters in Genesis 1:2, its only other use in the Torah.
b: Yerachef, "hovers, flutters," appears in the Torah only here and in Genesis 1:2, where God's Spirit hovers over the deep. The Song pictures God bringing Israel into being as he brought order to creation. Rashi explains the eagle: it rouses the nest gently, hovers without its full weight, and carries its young on its wings rather than in its claws, so that an arrow would hit the parent first. Exodus 19:4 uses the same image, and Jesus wishes to gather Jerusalem's children "the way a bird gathers her young under her wings" (Matthew 23:37).
orig: יְרַחֵף (yerachef), "it hovers, flutters"

a: He let him suck honey from the rock
p: Wild bees nest in clefts of rock, and olives grow on stony slopes: the land gives food even from stone.
b: In the hills of Israel wild bees build hives in rock crevices (Judges 14:8; 1 Samuel 14:25–27), and olive trees thrive in thin soil among rocks. The picture is of a land so rich that even its rock gives food. Psalm 81:16 repeats it: "I would fill you with honey from the rock." The rabbis and later Christian readers saw spiritual food in it, but the Song's point is God's lavish generosity, which Israel will repay with neglect (32:15).

a: Jeshurun
p: A rare pet name for Israel, from yashar, "upright." Here it is said with bitter irony.
b: Yeshurun appears only four times (32:15; 33:5, 26; Isaiah 44:2) and seems to mean "the upright one," from yashar. It sounds like "Israel." The Greek translates it "the beloved." The irony is sharp: the "upright one" grows fat and kicks like an overfed animal that no longer obeys its owner (compare 1 Samuel 2:29). Then the Song turns to "you" in a burst of three rhyming verbs, shamanta, avita, kasita, "you got fat, thick, stuffed."
orig: יְשֻׁרוּן (yeshurun)

a: They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God
p: The Hebrew shedim may come from Akkadian shedu, a protective spirit. Paul echoes the verse in 1 Corinthians 10:20.
b: Shedim appears only here and in Psalm 106:37, where Israel sacrifices its children to them. The word is probably related to Akkadian shedu, a guardian spirit, often shown as a winged bull at palace gates. Lo eloah can mean "not God" or "a no-god" (compare 32:21). The Greek has daimonia, "demons," and Paul says that what pagans sacrifice "they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20). So the Song treats other gods both as real spirit beings and as nothing compared with the LORD.
orig: יִזְבְּחוּ לַשֵּׁדִים לֹא אֱלֹהַּ (yizbechu lashedim lo eloah)

a: forgot the God who went into labor with you
p: The verb means to writhe in the pains of birth. The Song pictures God as Israel's father and mother.
b: Mecholelekha is from chul, to twist or writhe, used of a woman in labor (Isaiah 26:17; Psalm 29:9). The first line uses yalad, which can mean "father" or "give birth." So the Song gives God both a father's and a mother's part in Israel's birth. Isaiah also speaks of God crying out like a woman in labor (Isaiah 42:14) and comforting like a mother (Isaiah 66:13), and Moses asks whether he gave birth to this people (Numbers 11:12). English versions often soften the image.
orig: אֵל מְחֹלְלֶךָ (el mecholelekha), "the God who writhed in labor with you"
r: Isaiah 42:14; Isaiah 49:15; Isaiah 66:13; Numbers 11:12; Psalm 90:2; Isaiah 26:17; Psalm 29:9

a: angered me with their puffs of air
p: Hevel, "breath, vapor," is the word Ecclesiastes uses for "meaningless." Here it names idols.
b: Hevel is a breath you can see on a cold morning, there and then gone. Ecclesiastes uses it 38 times ("everything is hevel"), and the prophets use it for idols (Jeremiah 8:19; Jeremiah 10:8, 15; Jonah 2:8). The Song pairs it with "not-god": Israel has traded the Rock for vapor.
orig: בְּהַבְלֵיהֶם (behavlehem), "with their vapors"

a: So I will stir their jealousy with a not-people
p: Paul quotes this line in Romans 10:19 and builds Romans 11 on it: Gentile faith will make Israel jealous.
b: The Song's justice is measure for measure: Israel made God jealous with a "not-god," so God will make Israel jealous with a "not-people," probably a foreign enemy. Paul quotes it: "I myself will stir you to jealousy by those who are no nation. By a nation without understanding I will make you angry" (Romans 10:19). He reads "not-people" as the Gentiles who believe in Christ, and hopes that their faith will stir Israel to jealousy and so to salvation (Romans 11:11–14). Hosea 1:9–10 and 2:23, "not my people," are close in thought.
r: Romans 10:19; Romans 11:11–14; 1 Corinthians 10:22; Hosea 1:9–10; Hosea 2:23; Romans 9:25–26

a: that burns to the bottom of Sheol
p: Sheol is the world of the dead, under the earth. God's anger reaches even there.
b: She'ol tachtit, "lowest Sheol," is the deepest place imaginable, below the roots of the mountains. Sheol was the grave and the shadowy world where all the dead go (Genesis 37:35). Here God's anger burns like a fire through the whole universe, from the land's crops to the underworld. Psalm 139:8 makes the opposite point: even in Sheol God is there. Later Jewish and Christian writers connected the image with hell, but here it is a picture of a fire that nothing escapes.
orig: שְׁאוֹל תַּחְתִּית (she'ol tachtit), "lowest Sheol"

a: eaten up by burning plague and bitter sickness
p: Resheph was a Canaanite god of plague who shot arrows of disease. Here he is one of God's arrows.
b: The word for "burning plague" is resheph, the name of a Canaanite and Syrian god of plague and war, often shown with a bow, whose arrows spread disease. The Song has just spoken of God's arrows (32:23). Habakkuk 3:5 has Resheph marching at God's feet, and Psalm 78:48 uses the word for lightning bolts. Qetev, "sickness, destruction," became a demon in later Jewish lore, "the scourge that ravages at noon" (Psalm 91:6). Verdict: the names of old gods and demons have become the LORD's servants, forces he sends where he wills.

a: I will blow them away
p: The verb appears only here. Readers have guessed "scatter them," "cut them to pieces," or "Where are they?"
b: Af'ehem is found nowhere else. It may come from a root meaning "corner, edge," hence "scatter them to the corners" (KJV), or "blow away" (YLT), or "cut to pieces." The Sifre and Rashi split it into three words, af ei hem, "I said in anger: where are they?" Whatever the word, the next line is clear: God thought of wiping out Israel's memory from humankind, as he once threatened at the golden calf (9:14).
orig: אַפְאֵיהֶם (af'ehem)

a: except that I dreaded the enemy's taunts
t: For the sake of God's name
p: God spares Israel so that enemies will not boast. Moses had argued the same way at the golden calf.
b: God stops short of destroying Israel, not because Israel deserves mercy but because the enemy would take the credit. Moses used this argument in his prayers after the golden calf (9:28; Exodus 32:12) and the spies (Numbers 14:13–16). Ezekiel builds a whole theology on it: God acts "for the sake of my name, so that it would not be profaned among the nations" (Ezekiel 20:9, 14, 22; Ezekiel 36:20–23). Isaiah 48:9–11 says the same.

a: as even our enemies must judge
p: A short, puzzling line. It probably means that even Israel's enemies have to admit the LORD is stronger.
b: The Hebrew is just "and our enemies, judges" (pelilim). It may be an aside: "as our enemies themselves can judge," because they have seen what the LORD can do (compare Exodus 14:25; 1 Samuel 4:7–8). The Greek has "our enemies are fools." The point is the contrast in verse 30: if Israel loses battles, it is because Israel's Rock gave it up, not because the enemy's rock is stronger.
orig: וְאֹיְבֵינוּ פְּלִילִים (ve'oyvenu pelilim)

a: Their vine is a cutting from Sodom's vine
p: "They" may be Israel's enemies, ripe for judgment, or Israel itself, who has become like Sodom.
b: Verses 28–33 do not name their subject. Many read them as about the enemy nation (verse 27), proud and rotten like Sodom, whose turn for judgment is coming (verses 34–35). Others read them as about Israel, since Isaiah calls Jerusalem's rulers "rulers of Sodom" (Isaiah 1:10) and Jeremiah calls Israel a choice vine turned wild (Jeremiah 2:21). The words "if they were wise" (verse 29) sound like the lament over Israel's foolishness in verse 6.

a: Vengeance belongs to me, and payback
p: Paul and Hebrews quote this line in a form close to the Aramaic Targums: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay."
b: The Hebrew is li naqam veshillem, "to me belong vengeance and repayment." The Greek, like the Samaritan Pentateuch (leyom naqam), has "on the day of vengeance I will repay." Paul and Hebrews quote neither exactly: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19; Hebrews 10:30), a form close to the Targums. Paul uses it to tell believers not to take revenge but to leave room for God's justice and to feed their enemy. Naqam is not personal spite but the restoring of justice by the rightful ruler.
orig: לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלֵּם (li naqam veshillem)
r: Romans 12:19; Hebrews 10:30; Psalm 94:1; Nahum 1:2; Isaiah 34:8; Proverbs 20:22

a: for the time their foot slips
t: "Their foot shall slide in due time"
p: Jonathan Edwards preached his famous sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (1741) on this line.
b: In 1741, at Enfield, Connecticut, Jonathan Edwards took as his text the KJV "Their foot shall slide in due time." He argued that sinners stand on slippery ground, held up only by God's patience, "as one holds a spider over the fire." The sermon became the best-known product of the Great Awakening. In the Song the "foot" belongs to the enemy (verses 34–36), whose fall is near. Edwards applied the line to every person outside Christ.

a: The LORD will judge his people
p: Din can mean "judge" or "plead someone's case." Here God judges for his people, not against them.
b: Yadin means to give judgment, and often to win justice for someone (Genesis 30:6; Psalm 54:1). The next line, "and show his servants pity," shows that here God steps in to rescue Israel when its strength is gone. Psalm 135:14 repeats the verse in that sense. Hebrews 10:30 quotes "The Lord will judge his people" as a warning that God will judge those who reject his Son. Both senses belong to the word. "Held fast or set loose" is a pair meaning everyone, perhaps "slave or free."
orig: כִּי־יָדִין יְהוָה עַמּוֹ (ki yadin YHWH ammo)

a: Look now: I, only I, am he
p: God's "I, I am he" echoes through Isaiah, and the Greek "I am" lies behind some of Jesus' sayings in John.
b: Ani ani hu, "I, I am he," is the climax of the Song. Isaiah takes it up many times: "I am he. No god was shaped before me" (Isaiah 43:10–13; 41:4; 46:4; 48:12). The Greek renders it ego eimi, "I am," and in John's Gospel Jesus says, "unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins" and "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:24, 58). The line is also a strong statement of monotheism: "there is no god alongside me."
orig: אֲנִי אֲנִי הוּא (ani ani hu), "I, I am he"
r: Isaiah 41:4; Isaiah 43:10–13; Isaiah 45:5–7; Isaiah 46:4; Isaiah 48:12; John 8:24; John 8:58; John 18:5–6; 4:35; 4:39

a: I kill, and I make alive
p: The rabbis read the order as proof of resurrection: the same person God kills, God brings back to life.
b: Hannah's song echoes it: "The LORD kills and makes alive" (1 Samuel 2:6), and the king of Israel asks, "Am I God, able to kill and make alive?" (2 Kings 5:7). The Talmud asks: does it mean God kills one person and gives life to another? No: "I strike down and I make well" shows that the same person who is wounded is healed, so the same person who dies will live again (Pesachim 68a; Sanhedrin 91b). The verse is one of the Torah passages the rabbis used to teach the resurrection of the dead.

a: I lift my hand to the sky
p: A raised hand was the gesture of swearing an oath. God, who has no one greater to swear by, swears by his own life.
b: Abraham raised his hand to God when he swore (Genesis 14:22), and the angel in Daniel raises both hands to swear by the One who lives forever (Daniel 12:7). The angel of Revelation 10:5–6 does the same. God swears "As I live," the strongest oath possible, since there is no one higher to swear by (Hebrews 6:13). Ezekiel uses "As I live" for God's oaths many times.
r: Genesis 14:22; Exodus 6:8; Daniel 12:7; Revelation 10:5–6; Hebrews 6:13; Ezekiel 20:33

a: from the heads of the enemy's princes
p: Par'ot may mean "leaders" or "long locks," the uncut hair of warriors who had taken a vow.
b: Rosh par'ot oyev is literally "the head of the par'ot of the enemy." The same word appears in Judges 5:2, "When hair flies loose in Israel," often explained as warriors who let their hair grow during a holy war. So some translate "the long-haired heads of the enemy." Others relate it to a word for leaders, as the Plain English Translation does. The Greek has "rulers," which supports "princes." The KJV's "from the beginning of revenges upon the enemy" follows medieval Jewish readings of the word (Rashi, Ibn Ezra).
orig: מֵרֹאשׁ פַּרְעוֹת אוֹיֵב (merosh par'ot oyev)

a: this is not an empty word for you
t: "If it is empty, it is from you"
p: The Sifre reads "not empty from you": if the Torah seems empty, the emptiness comes from the reader.
b: The Hebrew lo davar req hu mikkem is literally "it is not an empty word from you." The Sifre, followed by Rashi, reads it as a warning: there is nothing empty in the Torah, and if it seems empty, it is because of you, who have not worked hard enough to understand it. The verse closes the Song with the same claim as 30:20: God's word is life itself. Jesus answers the tempter with 8:3, "People will not live by bread alone" (Matthew 4:4).
orig: לֹא דָבָר רֵק הוּא מִכֶּם (lo davar req hu mikkem)

a: Go up into these Abarim mountains, to Mount Nebo
p: A ridge in Jordan above the Jordan Valley. Pilgrims have visited a church of Moses there since the 4th century.
b: The Abarim ("those beyond") are the highlands east of the Dead Sea. Mount Nebo is usually identified with Ras es-Siyagha in Jordan, about 2,300 feet high, west of Madaba. From it you see the Dead Sea, the Jordan Valley, Jericho and, on clear days, the hills around Jerusalem. The pilgrim Egeria visited a church there in the 380s and was shown the place where Moses was believed to have died. Franciscan archaeologists excavated the Byzantine church and its mosaics from 1933. Numbers 27:12–14 gives the same command, a doublet critical scholars assign to the Priestly source.

a: be gathered to your people
p: An idiom for death that hints at joining the ancestors, even though Moses will be buried alone.
b: "Gathered to his people" is said of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and Aaron at their deaths (Genesis 25:8; Genesis 35:29; Genesis 49:33; Numbers 20:24). It once probably meant being laid in the family tomb, but Moses has no family tomb and Abraham was buried far from his ancestors. So many scholars think it came to mean joining the dead in Sheol, an early picture of a life with one's people after death. Aaron's death on Mount Hor is told in Numbers 20:22–29.
orig: וְהֵאָסֵף אֶל־עַמֶּיךָ (vehe'asef el ammekha), "and be gathered to your kin"
r: Genesis 25:8; Genesis 25:17; Genesis 35:29; Genesis 49:33; Numbers 20:24–29; Judges 2:10

a: For both of you acted unfaithfully toward me
p: Numbers 20 blames Moses' and Aaron's act at Meribah. Deuteronomy 1:37 says it was "because of you," the people.
b: The Hebrew me'altem, "you acted unfaithfully," is a strong word for breaking faith with God. Numbers 20:1–13 says Moses and Aaron did not believe God or show his holiness when Moses struck the rock. Yet 1:37, 3:26 and 4:21 say God was angry with Moses "because of you," the people. Readers explain the sin as striking instead of speaking (Rashi), as anger (Maimonides, Eight Chapters 4), or as speaking of "we" bringing water out (Numbers 20:10). Critical scholars see two traditions: one where Moses suffers for the people, one where he sins himself.

a: Moses the man of God
p: This is the first time Moses is called "the man of God," a title later given to prophets like Samuel and Elijah.
b: Ish ha'elohim names a prophet, someone who belongs to God and speaks for him (1 Samuel 9:6; 1 Kings 17:18; 2 Kings 4:9). Moses receives it here and in the heading of Psalm 90. A dying father blessing his sons is a Genesis scene: Isaac blesses Jacob and Esau (Genesis 27), and Jacob blesses his twelve sons (Genesis 49). Now Moses, the father of the nation, blesses the tribes. Simeon is missing from the list (see 33:6).
orig: אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים (ish ha'elohim)
r: Psalm 90:1; Joshua 14:6; 1 Samuel 9:6; 1 Kings 17:18; Genesis 27:1–40; Genesis 49:1–28

a: The LORD came from Sinai
p: Old poems have the LORD march from the southern deserts. An inscription near Sinai names "YHWH of Teman."
b: Sinai, Seir (Edom) and Mount Paran all lie south of Israel. The Song of Deborah (Judges 5:4–5), Habakkuk 3:3 ("God comes from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran") and Psalm 68:8 also picture God marching from the south. At Kuntillet Ajrud, a way station in northern Sinai from about 800 BC, inscriptions bless in the name of "YHWH of Teman" and "YHWH of Samaria." Many scholars take this as evidence that YHWH was first worshiped in the south, perhaps among Midianites or Kenites. Traditional readers see the memory of the journey from Sinai.

a: rose like the dawn over them from Seir
t: The Torah offered to the nations
p: The rabbis read Seir and Paran as Edom and Ishmael: God offered them the Torah first, and they refused.
b: Why does God come "from Seir" and "from Paran"? The Sifre answers with a famous midrash. God first offered the Torah to the children of Esau (Seir), who asked what was in it. Told "You must not murder," they refused, since their father lived by the sword. He offered it to Ishmael (Paran), who refused "You must not steal." Only Israel answered, "We will do and we will listen" (Exodus 24:7). The story explains Israel's choosing as Israel's acceptance (Sifre Deuteronomy 343; Avodah Zarah 2b).

a: and came from among ten thousands of holy ones
p: Later tradition said angels were present at Sinai. Jude quotes 1 Enoch, which uses these words of God's coming.
b: "Holy ones" (qodesh) are heavenly beings (Psalm 89:5–7; Zechariah 14:5). The Greek has "with myriads of Kadesh," reading a place name, and adds "angels with him at his right." Psalm 68:17 has thousands of chariots at Sinai. The New Testament says the law was given "through angels" (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). 1 Enoch 1:9 uses this verse for God coming to judge with ten thousands of holy ones, and Jude 14–15 quotes it.
r: Psalm 68:17; Zechariah 14:5; Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2; Jude 14–15; 1 Enoch 1:9

a: Yes, he loves the peoples
p: Every line of this verse is uncertain. "Peoples" may be the tribes of Israel or the nations.
b: Word for word: "Also loving peoples; all his holy ones in your hand; and they were led (or sat down) at your foot; he lifts from your words." "Peoples" can mean the tribes of Israel (Genesis 28:3; Genesis 48:4 "an assembly of peoples") or the nations of the world. "His holy ones" may be Israel or angels, and the shift from "his" to "your" is abrupt. The Greek reads "he spared his people." Rashi reads it as God's love for the tribes and Israel sitting at the foot of Sinai to receive his words. The Plain English Translation gives a likely sense.
orig: אַף חֹבֵב עַמִּים (af chovev ammim)

a: Moses commanded us a law
p: The Talmud says that as soon as a child can talk, his father should teach him this verse and the Shema.
b: "As soon as a child can speak, his father teaches him Torah and the Shema. What Torah? 'Moses commanded us a law, the heritage of the assembly of Jacob'" (Sukkah 42a). The rabbis also played on morashah, "heritage": do not read it "heritage" but me'orasah, "betrothed," for the Torah is Israel's bride (Pesachim 49b). Critics and some medieval readers notice that Moses is here spoken of as "Moses," which suggests that someone else voices the people's praise.
orig: תּוֹרָה צִוָּה־לָנוּ מֹשֶׁה מוֹרָשָׁה (torah tsivvah lanu moshe morashah)

a: He became king in Jeshurun
p: Most read God as king of Israel. Some take "he" as Moses. Jews read the verse in the New Year prayers of kingship.
b: The verse has no named subject. Most Jewish and Christian readers take it as God, acclaimed king when the tribes gathered at Sinai, as in "The LORD will be king forever and ever" (Exodus 15:18; compare Judges 8:23; 1 Samuel 8:7).
