Some interpreters, medieval and modern, take it as Moses, leader of the assembly. The verse is one of the ten "kingship" verses read in the additional prayer of Rosh Hashanah, which proclaims God king over the world.

a: though his men be few
p: The Hebrew is just "and let his men be a number." It can mean "few" or, with the negative carried on, "not few."
b: Vihi metav mispar is "let his men be a number," and in Hebrew "men you can number" means few (4:27; Genesis 34:30). The KJV and BSB carry the "not" of "not die" into this line: "let not his men be few." The Greek goes further: "let him be many in number." Either way, Reuben is weak, which fits its loss of the firstborn's place (Genesis 49:3–4) and its later fading from history east of the Jordan. Simeon is missing from Moses' blessing altogether; later Simeon was absorbed into Judah (Joshua 19:1–9). A few Greek manuscripts add, "and let Simeon be great in number."
orig: וִיהִי מְתָיו מִסְפָּר (vihi metav mispar)

a: and bring him to his people
p: Is Judah fighting far away, or cut off from the other tribes, as after the kingdom split? Readers differ.
b: The prayer is that Judah be heard and brought back to "his people." Some read it as Judah at war, needing help and a safe return. Others read it in the light of history: Judah cut off from the northern tribes, after the kingdom divided in about 930 BC (1 Kings 12), which would date this line. Rashi connects it with Reuben just before: Judah, who confessed his sin with Tamar, led Reuben to confess too, and both were "brought to their people" (Sotah 7b). Jacob's blessing gave Judah the scepter (Genesis 49:8–12); Moses' blessing is far shorter.

a: your Thummim, and your Urim
p: The priest's lots, here named in reverse order. The Levites' right to use them is their chief blessing.
b: The Urim and Thummim were objects kept in the high priest's breastpiece and used to learn God's will by lot (Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 14:41). Only here does Thummim come first. The blessing gives Levi the priest's duties: guiding by the lots, teaching the law and offering sacrifice (33:10). Massah and Meribah recall the tests at the water (Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:1–13), where Moses and Aaron, Levites, were tested.
orig: תֻּמֶּיךָ וְאוּרֶיךָ (tummekha ve'urekha)

a: He said of his father and mother, 'I have not seen them.'
p: After the golden calf the Levites killed even their own kin. Jesus asks for a love greater than for family.
b: At the golden calf Moses called, "Whoever is on the LORD's side, to me!" and the Levites came and struck down the guilty, even brothers and neighbors (Exodus 32:26–29). Their reward was the priesthood. In the blessing, loyalty to God's covenant outranks father, mother, brothers and children. Jesus makes a similar demand: whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him (Matthew 10:37; Luke 14:26).

a: They will teach your rulings to Jacob
p: Levi's first task is teaching. The prophets blame priests who fail at it.
b: Priests were to teach Israel the difference between holy and common and all God's rules (Leviticus 10:10–11; 17:9–11; 24:8). Malachi praises Levi: "True teaching was in his mouth ... people look to his mouth for teaching" (Malachi 2:6–7), and Hosea condemns priests who forgot God's law (Hosea 4:6). Teaching comes before sacrifice in this blessing.

a: and he rests between his shoulders
p: The rabbis read the temple into this verse: Jerusalem lay on Benjamin's border, "between his shoulders."
b: The pronouns are unclear: who rests between whose shoulders? One reading: Benjamin, God's beloved, is carried on God's shoulders like a child. Another: God dwells between Benjamin's "shoulders," that is, his mountain slopes. Jerusalem lay on the border of Benjamin and Judah (Joshua 15:8; Joshua 18:16, 28), and the rabbis held that the temple altar stood on Benjamin's land (Zevachim 53b–54b; Yoma 12a). Benjamin, Jacob's youngest and best-loved son by Rachel, is the "beloved" (Genesis 44:20).
r: Joshua 15:8; Joshua 18:16; Joshua 18:28; Genesis 44:20; Genesis 49:27; Isaiah 46:3–4

a: and of the deep that lies stretched out below
p: Tehom, "the deep," the waters under the earth, is pictured as an animal lying down. Jacob's blessing of Joseph says the same.
b: Joseph's land is blessed with water from above (dew) and from below (springs fed by tehom, the deep). The deep "crouches" (rovetset) like an animal. Jacob's blessing of Joseph uses the same words, "blessings of the deep that lies below" (Genesis 49:25), and some scholars emend mittal, "from the dew," to me'al, "from above," to match it. Tehom is related to Akkadian tiamtum, "sea," and to Tiamat, the sea monster of the Babylonian creation story. Verdict: the words are related, but in the Bible the deep is no rival god, only a source of water God controls.
orig: וּמִתְּהוֹם רֹבֶצֶת תָּחַת (umittehom rovetset tachat)

a: and the favor of the one who lived in the bush
t: The one who lived in the bush
p: The only mention of the burning bush outside Exodus 3. Seneh, "bush," sounds like Sinai.
b: Shokheni seneh, "the one who dwelt in the bush," recalls Exodus 3:2–4, where God called Moses from a burning thorn bush. The word seneh sounds like "Sinai," and some scholars think the two were once connected. Joseph is called nezir echav, "the one set apart from his brothers," as in Genesis 49:26, either because he was separated from them in Egypt or because he became their leader. Nazir is also the word for a Nazirite.
orig: שֹׁכְנִי סְנֶה (shokheni seneh), "the dweller of the bush"

a: his horns are a wild ox's horns
p: The KJV says "unicorns." The Hebrew re'em is the wild ox, the aurochs, now extinct.
b: The Greek translators rendered re'em as monokeros, "one-horned," and the KJV followed with "unicorns"; Jerome here has "rhinoceros." But the verse speaks of horns in the plural, and the animal is the wild ox (aurochs), a huge, fierce bull known from Assyrian hunting scenes, extinct since 1627. Joseph's "firstborn bull" is Ephraim, and the bull image may connect with the bull statues Jeroboam of Ephraim set up at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–29).
orig: קַרְנֵי רְאֵם (qarne re'em), "the horns of a wild ox"
r: Numbers 23:22; Numbers 24:8; Job 39:9–12; Psalm 22:21; Psalm 92:10; 1 Kings 12:28–29

a: and the treasures hidden in the sand
t: Dye and glass from Zebulun's shore
p: The Talmud says Zebulun's coast gave the snail for blue-violet dye and the sand for glass.
b: Zebulun and Issachar lay in the north, near the Mediterranean and the Valley of Jezreel. The Talmud explains "the wealth of the seas" as the chilazon, the sea snail used for blue-violet (tekhelet) dye, and "the treasures hidden in the sand" as white glass made from the coastal sand (Megillah 6a). Glassmaking did flourish on that coast in Roman times. Rashi reads "Rejoice, Zebulun, when you go out, and Issachar, in your tents" as a partnership: Zebulun traded by sea and supported Issachar, who studied Torah in tents.

a: for a ruler's share was kept for him there
p: The rabbis and the Targum read "ruler" as "lawgiver," Moses, buried in Gad's land.
b: Mechoqeq can mean "commander" or "lawgiver." Gad chose land east of the Jordan before the conquest (Numbers 32), and Targum Onqelos and Rashi say the "lawgiver's portion" there is the grave of Moses, the great lawgiver, which lay in the territory Gad received. The Talmud uses this verse to say that Moses was buried in Gad's land, though he died on Nebo in Reuben's (Sotah 13b). Gad then "came with the heads of the people," crossing the Jordan to fight with the other tribes (Numbers 32:20–22; Joshua 4:12).
orig: חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק (chelqat mechoqeq), "the portion of a commander or lawgiver"

a: Dan is a lion's cub
p: Jacob called Judah a lion's cub and Dan a snake. Moses calls Dan the lion's cub, leaping from Bashan.
b: In Genesis 49:9 Judah is "a lion's cub," and Dan is a snake by the road (Genesis 49:17). Moses gives Dan the lion's image. Bashan lay far to the northeast, near the territory Dan took when it moved north to Laish (Judges 18:27–29). Critical scholars see in the line a time after that migration. Samson, the famous Danite, fought with a lion (Judges 14:5–6).

a: and may he dip his foot in oil
p: Asher's land in western Galilee was rich in olives. The Talmud says oil ran there like a river.
b: Asher lived in the hills and coast of western Galilee, among the best olive country in the land. "Dipping the foot in oil" is a picture of plenty: so much oil that you could wade in it. The Talmud tells of a buyer from Laodicea who found the oil of Gush Halav, in Asher's land, so abundant that a man could fill whole vats (Menachot 85b). Job remembers when his "feet waded in curds, / and the rock poured streams of oil" (Job 29:6).

a: The bolts of your gates will be iron and bronze
p: The KJV reads "Thy shoes shall be iron and brass." The Hebrew word means "bolt" or "lock."
b: Min'al is a door bolt or lock, from the verb "to lock" (Judges 3:23). The KJV connected it with na'al, "sandal," hence "Thy shoes shall be iron and brass." Asher's border towns faced Phoenicia and the north, so strong gates mattered. The second line, ukhyamekha dov'ekha, has a word found nowhere else. "Your strength will be as your days" (KJV "as thy days, so shall thy strength be") is a common guess; others suggest "your rest" or "your wealth."
orig: בַּרְזֶל וּנְחֹשֶׁת מִנְעָלֶךָ (barzel unechoshet min'alekha)

a: He rides across the sky to help you
p: In texts from Ugarit, Baal is called "Rider of the Clouds." The Bible gives the title to the LORD.
b: In the Baal myths from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), the storm god is called rkb 'rpt, "rider of the clouds." Psalm 68:4 calls God "the one who rides through the deserts," often taken as a play on the same title, and Psalm 104:3 makes the clouds his chariot. Isaiah 19:1 has the LORD ride a swift cloud into Egypt. Daniel 7:13 has "one like a son of man" coming with the clouds, the image Jesus uses of himself (Mark 14:62). Verdict: a real link; Israel's poets claimed the storm god's title for the LORD alone.
r: Psalm 68:4; Psalm 68:33; Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1; Daniel 7:13; Mark 14:62

a: No one is like God, Jeshurun!
p: The Hebrew vowels make Jeshurun the one spoken to. With other vowels, it reads "none like the God of Jeshurun."
b: The Masoretic Text points the words en ka'el yeshurun, "there is none like God, O Jeshurun," and the Plain English Translation follows it. The Greek, the Vulgate and many modern versions read the same letters as ke'el yeshurun, "none like the God of Jeshurun," which matches the third-person praise that follows. The consonants are the same; only the vowels differ. Either way, the line returns to the name Jeshurun, "the upright one," from 32:15 and 33:5.
orig: אֵין כָּאֵל יְשֻׁרוּן (en ka'el yeshurun)

a: and beneath are arms that last forever
p: A much-loved line, made famous by the KJV and the hymn "Leaning on the Everlasting Arms." The Hebrew is uncertain.
b: The words umittachat zero'ot olam are literally "and from beneath, arms of eternity." Most take them as God's arms holding his people up from below, and the 1887 hymn "Leaning on the Everlasting Arms" made the KJV wording beloved. The first line, me'onah elohei qedem, may also mean "a dwelling is the God of old." Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman proposed a different text: he subdues the ancient gods and shatters the powers of old, which fits the next line about driving out the enemy. The Plain English Translation keeps the received text.
orig: וּמִתַּחַת זְרֹעֹת עוֹלָם (umittachat zero'ot olam)

a: Jacob's spring stands apart
p: Balaam said Israel is "a people that settles by itself." Moses' last blessing says the same.
b: Badad, "alone, apart," echoes Balaam's oracle: "Here is a people that settles by itself, and does not count itself one of the nations" (Numbers 23:9). Living "alone" here means in safety, with no enemy near (Jeremiah 49:31). "Jacob's spring" may mean Jacob's descendants, flowing from him like water from a spring (Psalm 68:26; Isaiah 48:1). Jewish thinkers have often reflected on Israel as "a people that dwells alone" among the nations.

a: How happy you are, Israel!
p: The word that opens Psalm 1 and the Beatitudes. It is not the same as "blessed by God."
b: Ashrekha means "your happiness, how fortunate you are!" It is different from barukh, "blessed," used when God or someone else pronounces a blessing. Ashrei opens Psalm 1 ("How happy is the one who does not walk ...") and many other psalms, and the Greek makarios that renders it opens each of Jesus' Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–11). The Torah's last poem ends on Israel's good fortune: no one is like Israel, because no one is like Israel's God (33:26).
orig: אַשְׁרֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל (ashrekha yisra'el)

a: and you will tread on their high places
p: Bamot can mean hilltops, hill shrines, or the backs of defeated enemies.
b: Bamot usually means "heights," or hilltop shrines (the "high places" of Kings). An Ugaritic cognate means "back," and conquerors did put their feet on the backs or necks of defeated kings (Joshua 10:24). So the line may mean "you will trample their backs." God himself treads the heights of the earth (Amos 4:13; Micah 1:3), and Israel shares that victory (32:13; Isaiah 58:14).
orig: עַל־בָּמוֹתֵימוֹ תִדְרֹךְ (al bamotemo tidrokh)

a: There the LORD let him see the whole land
p: From Nebo you cannot see Dan or the Mediterranean. Was this a miracle, a legal act, or a summary of the land?
b: The list runs from Gilead and Dan in the north, west across Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, south through Judah to the Negev, and back to Jericho and Zoar, a full circle of the land. Much of it is not visible from Nebo. The Sifre and Rashi say God showed Moses the whole land, and its whole future history, by a miracle. David Daube suggested a legal custom: to view a property formally was to take possession of it, as when God told Abram to look north, south, east and west (Genesis 13:14–15). Others read the list as a writer's summary of the land.

a: 'I will give it to your offspring.'
p: The Torah ends with the promise to Abraham not yet fulfilled. The people stand on the edge of the land.
b: God's oath to Abraham (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 15:18), Isaac (Genesis 26:3) and Jacob (Genesis 28:13) is repeated as the last word to Moses. The five books of Moses end outside the land. David Clines argued that the theme of the whole Pentateuch is the partial fulfillment of the promise to the patriarchs: offspring, relationship with God, and land, with the land still ahead. Jews have read the ending as a lesson that the Torah, not the land, is what made Israel a people; Christians, like Hebrews 11:13–16, as a sign that the final homeland is still to come.
r: Genesis 12:7; Genesis 15:18–21; Genesis 26:3; Genesis 28:13; Hebrews 11:13–16; Hebrews 4:8–9

a: Moses the servant of the LORD
p: Eved YHWH, "the LORD's servant," is a title of honor, like a king's trusted minister, not a word for a lowly slave.
b: Eved can mean slave, servant or royal official, depending on context. "Servant of the LORD" is the highest title Moses receives, used of him again and again in Joshua (Joshua 1:1, 13, 15) and later (2 Kings 18:12). It is also given to David and to the mysterious servant of Isaiah 42–53. Hebrews 3:5 says Moses was faithful "as a servant" in God's house, while Christ is faithful as a son. Revelation 15:3 has the redeemed sing "the song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb."
orig: עֶבֶד־יְהוָה (eved YHWH)
r: Joshua 1:1; Joshua 1:13; 2 Kings 18:12; Isaiah 42:1; Hebrews 3:5; Revelation 15:3; Numbers 12:7

a: at the LORD's word
p: Literally "by the mouth of the LORD." The rabbis said Moses died by God's kiss.
b: Al pi YHWH usually means "by the LORD's command," but literally it is "on the mouth of the LORD." The rabbis took it literally: Moses died by a kiss from God, as did Aaron (Numbers 33:38, where the same Hebrew phrase is used) and Miriam (Bava Batra 17a; Mo'ed Katan 28a). Later midrash tells how Moses argued with God for his life, and how God himself took Moses' soul with a kiss. The phrase "death by a kiss" became the Jewish image of the most peaceful death.
orig: עַל־פִּי יְהוָה (al pi YHWH), "on the mouth of the LORD"

a: And he buried him
p: "He" can only be God. The rabbis drew from it the duty to bury the dead, as God did.
b: No human is named, and verse 6 adds that no one knows the grave, so the plain reading is that God buried Moses. The Talmud teaches that following the LORD (13:4) means imitating his ways. As he clothed the naked (Genesis 3:21), visited the sick (Genesis 18:1) and comforted mourners (Genesis 25:11), and as he buried the dead, as it says, "he buried him in the valley," so you must bury the dead (Sotah 14a). Some ancient versions read "they buried him" (see the variant).

a: No one knows the place of his grave to this day
p: "To this day" looks back from a later time. Tradition and critics both say someone other than Moses wrote these verses.
b: Could Moses write about his own death? The Talmud gives two views: Joshua wrote the last eight verses (34:5–12), or Moses wrote them at God's dictation, in tears (Bava Batra 15a; Menachot 30a). Philo and Josephus say Moses foresaw and wrote his own death; Josephus adds that he did so lest people say he had gone up to God alive (Antiquities 4.326). Abraham ibn Ezra held that Joshua wrote from 34:1 on, and hinted at other later additions (on 1:2), and Spinoza took "to this day" as proof of later authorship. The unknown grave may also guard against a shrine of Moses-worship.

a: facing Beth-peor
p: Moses was buried near the place where Israel sinned with the Baal of Peor.
b: Beth-peor, "the house of Peor," was near the place where Israel worshiped the Baal of Peor and suffered a plague (Numbers 25:1–9). The rabbis said Moses' grave was placed facing Peor to make atonement for that sin (Sotah 14a). Jude 9 refers to a dispute between Michael and the devil over Moses' body, probably from a lost ending of the Assumption of Moses. At the transfiguration Moses appears with Elijah, talking with Jesus (Matthew 17:3).

a: his vigor had not drained away
p: Le'ach, "moisture, freshness," is used of a green branch. Moses died with his sap still in him.
b: Lecho, from le'ach, "moisture," describes something fresh and green (Genesis 30:37, "fresh" branches). Old age dries a person out, but Moses' eyes and body were still sound at 120. So he did not die of age or sickness, but because his time had come. On the tension with 31:2, see the note there.
orig: לֹא־נָס לֵחֹה (lo nas lecho), "his moisture had not fled"

a: for thirty days
p: Israel mourned Moses thirty days, as it had Aaron. Jewish custom keeps a thirty-day mourning period, the sheloshim.
b: Aaron too was mourned thirty days (Numbers 20:29), and the captive woman of 21:13 mourns her parents a full month. Egypt mourned Jacob seventy days (Genesis 50:3). Jewish law sets the sheloshim, the first thirty days after burial, as a period of lighter mourning after the first week (shiva), drawing on this verse.

a: Moses had laid his hands on Joshua son of Nun
p: Moses' hands on Joshua (Numbers 27:18–23) became the model for Jewish semikhah and Christian ordination.
b: In Numbers 27:18–23 God tells Moses to lay his hand on Joshua, "a man in whom is the spirit," before the priest and the people. Here the act fills Joshua with "a spirit of wisdom." The rabbis called the ordination of a teacher semikhah, "leaning (of hands)," tracing a chain from Moses to Joshua to the elders (Mishnah Avot 1:1). The church laid hands on the Seven (Acts 6:6), on Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:3) and on Timothy (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6).
r: Numbers 27:18–23; Acts 6:6; Acts 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6; Isaiah 11:2

a: No prophet has risen again in Israel like Moses
p: 18:15 promised "a prophet like me." This verse says none had come. Jews and Christians read the tension differently.
b: In 18:15–18 Moses promises that God will raise up "a prophet like me." These lines, written looking back, say that none has yet arisen. Jewish tradition holds that none ever will: Maimonides' seventh principle of faith is that Moses' prophecy was greater than any other, and the hymn Yigdal sings, "No one has arisen in Israel like Moses." The New Testament presents Jesus as the promised prophet (Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37; John 6:14) and as greater than Moses (Hebrews 3:3). The Samaritans also await a prophet like Moses, the Taheb.
r: 18:15–18; Numbers 12:6–8; Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37; John 1:21; John 6:14; Hebrews 3:1–6

a: whom the LORD knew face to face
p: No one could see God's face and live (Exodus 33:20), yet the LORD spoke with Moses "face to face."
b: Exodus 33:11 says the LORD spoke to Moses "face to face, as anyone talks with a close companion," and Numbers 12:8 says "mouth to mouth." Yet Exodus 33:20 says no one can see God's face and live. The phrase describes closeness, not a sight of God's full glory. Paul hopes that believers will one day see "face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12), and Revelation promises that God's servants "will see his face" (Revelation 22:4).

a: in the sight of all Israel
t: From the last letter to the first
p: The Torah ends with "Israel." Rashi says "in the sight of all Israel" means the breaking of the tablets.
b: The last word of the Torah is Yisra'el, and its last letter is lamed; the first letter of Genesis is bet. Together they spell lev, "heart." Rashi, following the Sifre, says that the "great and fearful deeds" done "in the sight of all Israel" refer to Moses smashing the tablets before their eyes (9:17), and that God approved. On the holiday of Simchat Torah, Jews read these last verses and then begin Genesis 1 at once, so that the reading of the Torah never ends.
